title: Book 4 — Melpomene, Chapter 201
paragraphs: As they continued to suffer hardship for a long time, and many were falling on both sides—but most of all on the Persian side—Amasis, commander of the land-army, devised the following scheme. Realizing that the Barcaeans could not be conquered by force but might be conquered by cunning, he dug by night a broad trench, laid over it timber of no great strength, and then brought earth and heaped it on top of the timber, leveling it with the rest of the ground. At daybreak he invited the Barcaeans to a parley; and they gladly consented, and in the end they agreed to make a treaty. The treaty was sworn over the hidden trench, to this effect: that so long as this earth remained as it was, the oath would remain firm; that the Barcaeans would agree to pay a reasonable tribute to the king; and that the Persians would do no further violence to the Barcaeans. After the oath, the Barcaeans, trusting these pledges, went out of their city themselves and allowed any of the enemy who wished to pass inside the walls, having opened all the gates. But the Persians first broke down the concealed bridge and then ran inside the city wall. And the reason they broke down the bridge they had made was so that they might keep their oath, since they had sworn to the Barcaeans that the oath would remain firm as long as the earth remained as it then was; once they had broken it down, the oath no longer held.
